title: File timestamps: MACB
quick: File timestamps record when a file was modified, accessed, changed or born. MACB is the short name for these four times, and each file system stores them differently.

sections.title: The four times
text: M is modified: the content last changed. A is accessed: the file was last read or opened. C is changed: the metadata record of the file was last changed (in NTFS this is the MFT entry modified time). B is born: the file was created on this volume.
Not every file system keeps all four. FAT has no change time. Older Linux file systems have no birth time. Names also vary between tools, so check the tool help.

sections.title: Precision and behaviour
text: Precision differs. FAT stores last modified with a two second step. NTFS uses a count of 100 nanosecond units. ext4 and APFS record times with nanosecond detail.

Copying or moving a file can change times in different ways. Copying usually gives the new file a new creation time, while the modified time may stay. Recent Windows versions do not update last access by default, so it may not show real reading.

sections.title: Reading times with care
text: The system clock can be wrong or not synchronised. Time zone and daylight saving settings also matter, because some systems store local time and others store UTC. A user or a tool can also change times on purpose.
Treat a timestamp as one clue and compare it with other sources, such as logs, the USN journal and the file content. Record the time zone you used in your notes.

example: A document appears to have been created on Monday, but the modified time is earlier. The examiner sees that the file was copied from a USB drive. The creation time shows the copy time on this volume, while the modified time kept the original value.
mistakes: Assuming access time shows when a user read the file.
Ignoring time zones and mixing local time with UTC.
Trusting the system clock without checking it.
Using a tool that shows only one of the four times.

terms.meaning: Modified, Accessed, Changed, Born, the four common file times.
Coordinated Universal Time, a time standard without daylight saving.
A recorded date and time attached to data.
A list of events ordered by time.

exam.q: Why can a copied file have a creation time later than its modified time?
exam.a: The copy is a new file on the new volume, so it gets a new creation time, while the modified time can be carried over.

exam.q: Why must you be careful with the system clock?
exam.a: If the clock was wrong or not synchronised, the recorded times are wrong too. Compare with other time sources.
